assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped how economists understand who trades, who gains and how aggregate productivity responds to openness. The framework changed both theory and empirical practice, and it is the standard foundation for modern trade analysis. It is a conceptual advance with measurable consequences.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the core model and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) the key extension to exporting versus FDI. Helpman also contributed foundational work across trade theory. Redding's contribution is substantial but more focused on quantitative and spatial extensions, so the strongest credit lies with Helpman and Melitz.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of testing, replication and extension in many countries and data sets. The field has not been recognised since 2008, so the timing is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Helpman paired with Grossman (political economy of protection and growth) to this pairing.
Whether Redding or others should share credit.
My knowledge of the finer attribution in heterogeneous-firm trade is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data turned intergenerational mobility into a precisely measured, geographically resolved object. It reshaped debates on opportunity, place effects and policy evaluation. Method and substance are both influential, and the data-building ethos is strongly valued in economic history as well.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear intellectual leader. Hendren (neighbourhood and exposure effects) and Friedman (tax-record based mobility and teacher value-added) are central co-contributors. Katz's role is important but more tied to earlier mobility and experiment work.
assessment.maturity: The central results are from roughly 2014 to 2022 and are replicated in several countries, but long-run validation, such as policy effects on actual mobility, is still maturing.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is yet seen as a distinct paradigm versus a very productive empirical program.
Causal interpretation of place effects and the trade-offs among the many co-authors.
Age and timing: the committee may wait for further confirmation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantile regression moved empirical work beyond conditional means to whole distributions, which is essential for analysing inequality, wage structure and heterogeneous effects. It is a fundamental, widely used method across fields, including labour, finance, growth and economic history.
assessment.attribution: Koenker and Bassett (1978) introduced the estimator, and Koenker developed the inference theory, computation and applications over decades. Chernozhukov's contributions (instrumental quantile regression, counterfactual distributions) are major but overlap with other candidates and could be recognised elsewhere.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: nearly five decades of use, standard in textbooks and software. Recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Econometric-method prizes depend on how the committee values pure methods versus substantive discoveries.
Whether Chernozhukov should be included instead of Bassett.
Possible age or health constraints on the earliest contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run, tax-record based series on top incomes and wealth rebuilt the empirical basis for discussing inequality, with a distributional national accounts program built on top. This is a measurement contribution of the first order and it changed public and academic debate. The historical-data approach fits the best tradition of archival economics.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez (2003) is the foundational top-income paper and Zucman extended the work to offshore wealth and distributional accounts. The World Inequality Database involves many collaborators, so credit is diffuse beyond these three. Atkinson, who is deceased, was a key pioneer.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work has been replicated in many countries, while the wealth-tax, offshore and capital-return interpretations remain debated.
uncertainties: Contested methodological choices in wealth estimation and the interpretation of r > g.
Whether the committee sees the work as measurement or as theory.
Policy-advocacy profile may weigh on committee dynamics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock research showed that trade shocks can have persistent, geographically concentrated labour-market effects, challenging the assumption of smooth adjustment. Autor's task-based work links technology, polarisation and wage inequality. This ties closely to the societal transitions that the Committee has recently honoured.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the core authors of the China-shock papers, with Autor central to the task and polarisation literature. Katz is a key co-author on earlier skill-demand work, and Acemoglu has already been recognised for related themes.
assessment.maturity: Substantial evidence since about 2013, with extensions and critiques over the past decade. The long-run durability of the effects continues to be studied.
uncertainties: Debate over the identification strategy and the size of the effects.
Partial overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes in technology and growth themes.
Whether the tasks and trade-shock strands form one coherent prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers model gave bargaining a tractable non-cooperative foundation, linking patience and outside options to outcomes. It underlies work on labour, markets, politics and negotiation. It is a core theoretical advance that is conceptually clean and durable.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the seminal result. Binmore, Rubinstein and Wolinsky (1986) tie the model to market outcomes and Binmore contributed key extensions and interpretation. Stahl and Ståhl-type precursors and later markets-with-search work make exact credit allocation less tidy.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use. Recognition is plausible at any time, though game theory and mechanism design have recently been honoured (2020 and others).
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a game-theory prize for another topic.
Allocation among Rubinstein, Binmore and Wolinsky.
Limited direct empirical validation relative to impact on theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A centuries-long quantitative record of banking crises, sovereign default and inflation reframed crisis analysis as a recurring historical pattern. It is archival, data-driven and highly influential on policy and research agendas. The 2022 prize recognised the theory of banks and crises, and this work would complement it empirically.
assessment.attribution: The joint authorship of the main database and the book This Time Is Different is clear. Reinhart and Rogoff each have additional independent contributions (Rogoff on exchange rates, Reinhart on capital flows and sudden stops).
assessment.maturity: The central database dates from about 2009 and is widely used. Nonetheless, subsequent critiques are part of the record.
uncertainties: The 2013 controversy over the debt-and-growth threshold result, which is a separate paper but may colour perceptions.
Whether the committee values data compilation and synthesis enough for a prize.
Causal claims about crises are weaker than the descriptive ones.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: GMM estimators for dynamic panels solved a basic practical problem of estimating persistence with unobserved heterogeneity. They became standard across growth, labour, finance and industrial organisation. The impact is broad and the methods are used daily, though the contribution is more specialised than a core conceptual advance.
assessment.attribution: Arellano and Bond (1991), Arellano and Bover (1995) and Blundell and Bond (1998) are the central papers. Blundell has additional prize-relevant work in labour supply and taxation. The credit is clear for the three, but overlaps with Hansen's GMM (already recognised in 2013).
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with widespread use and a known literature on weak-instrument and many-instrument problems.
uncertainties: Known limitations, such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments, mean the methods are sometimes misused.
Competing econometric candidates, such as quantile regression, may be preferred by the committee.
Whether the committee would see it as a major discovery or as a refinement of GMM.
